claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
Introducing a small amount of interstitial elements can preserve toughness after thermal exposure and subsequent loading.
Carbon is a suitable interstitial addition for the proposed intervention.
Carbon addition can enhance solid-solution strengthening.
Carbon addition can refine the alloy's grains.
The applicable thermal exposure is 500 °C for 2 hours.
Loading consists of uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature after thermal exposure.
Grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening lead to improved toughness.
The interstitial-modified alloy will have better toughness than the alloy without interstitial additions.
The interstitial-modified alloy will exhibit a 10% increase in elongation relative to the unmodified alloy.
The interstitial-modified alloy will exhibit a 5% decrease in yield strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
The unmodified alloy has a yield strength of 800 MPa under the stated conditions.
The unmodified alloy has an elongation of 20% under the stated conditions.
The interstitial addition will not produce brittle phases.
The intervention and thermal exposure will not significantly degrade the alloy microstructure.
The outcome may depend on alloy composition, processing route, and the amount and type of interstitial addition.
A decrease in elongation in the modified alloy relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
An increase in yield strength in the modified alloy relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is said to enhance solid-solution strengthening, but the predicted outcome is a 5% decrease in yield strength. The cited carbon observation likewise reports a higher strength effect rather than a reduction.
An increase in yield strength is defined as falsifying, even though the proposed solid-solution-strengthening mechanism would ordinarily predict an increase in resistance to yielding.
